items.title: BL-203's predictive spending is bimodal in practice, not graded — the taper band has zero occupancy because market demand runs 2-3 orders of magnitude below supply
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI gameplay session; measured from --export-blackboard all --ticks 30 on the default seed.
items.what: forecast_glut_multiplier is designed as a graded taper: no penalty at supply/demand <= glut_taper_ratio (1.0), linear taper to a veto at glut_veto_ratio (2.0). Measured against a real 30-tick rollout, it is a coin flip between OFF and VETO instead. Of one rival's 64 (market, resource) supply slots at tick 30: 6 carry both supply > 0 and demand > 0, and ALL SIX sit at supply/demand between 78 and 339 — every one at or past the veto threshold; 5 carry supply with demand == 0, where the design deliberately applies no penalty at all (the AI cannot forecast against a fact it cannot see); the taper band between 1.0 and 2.0 has ZERO occupancy. Across all corps the same shape holds: 1728 demand facts of which 324 are non-zero with a maximum of 8.25, against supply reaching 15,141. This was found by trying to damp the NR-178 idle/resume cycle with the same forecast and measuring no change whatsoever on any of the five benchmark seeds — the change was reverted rather than kept as an unverified behaviour change.
items.why_it_matters: AI_OPPONENT.md section 4 calls the Victoria-3 predictive-spending model 'the single most important design import' and section 2B describes a taper. What is actually running is a binary gate, and which way it falls is decided by whether a demand aggregate happens to be non-zero rather than by any economic reasoning. That plausibly explains the AI's very low build rate (3-6 builds per 30-tick rollout across ten corps). The prior question is not an AI question at all: why does market demand max out around 8 while supply reaches 15,000? Either the two aggregates are not commensurable (a per-tick flow compared against a stock would produce exactly this), in which case the ratio is meaningless and the veto is firing on a unit error, or the world genuinely has almost no demand and the economy is the thing to look at. Both readings make the current veto wrong; they differ in what to fix.
options: Check commensurability first — establish what market_component.supply and .demand each accumulate per tick before touching any AI threshold. If they are flow-vs-stock the fix is in market_clearing, not corp_ai.
Re-scale glut_taper_ratio / glut_veto_ratio to the observed distribution so the taper band actually spans real ratios.
Treat demand == 0 as a veto rather than a pass, inverting the current 'cannot see it, so no penalty' rule.
Leave it — the AI is solvent and survives, so the gate's shape is not currently costing anything visible.
items.recommendation: Option 1, and nothing else until it is answered. Re-scaling thresholds against a ratio that may be a unit error would bake the error into the AI's tuning, and this is exactly the pattern SPRINTS.md records overturning four times last sprint — the plausible story (the AI is cautious) and the measured cause (the comparison may not be a comparison) point at different files.
items.resolution:
ANSWERED 2026-08-13, and the answer is neither of the two options this entry offered.

NOT a stock/flow unit error at the field level. Both arrays are zeroed together at the top of every clear_markets — the only reset site in the codebase — and both nominally count units through the market this tick. The obvious hypothesis is refuted.

The ratio is nonetheless a NON-MEASURE, for four compounding reasons, and no threshold can repair it:

0. CORRECTED after adversarial verification of this very answer, and recorded rather than silently edited. The first write-up said the gate 'fires on nonsense' and was 'non-functional', and quoted '81% of slots carry supply against demand == 0'. The figure was mis-derived — 81% is the share of ALL demand facts that are zero, while the share of SUPPLY-BEARING slots with no demand is about 45% (5 of 11 in the sampled rival) — and it was quoted three times. The framing was also too strong: resolve_price floors at 0.25x base and the observed slots are pegged there, so oversupply DOES already reach the AI through the profit estimate. The accurate charge is that the gate is NON-DISCRIMINATING (every demand-bearing slot is past veto, so it cannot rank anything) and silent exactly where no consumer exists.
1. Supply is unbounded by demand BY CONSTRUCTION. clear_markets is an unconditional buyer of last resort — every listed unit sells at the reference price whatever demand says — while three of the five demand writers are notional and buy nothing. The two arrays are not two sides of one book.
2. Only 12 of 42 resources have any standing consumer, and NO RAW ORE has one. A glut of iron ore is structurally invisible to this gate, which is precisely the glut the scorer's build candidate is most likely to create, since it only ever proposes extraction sites.
3. The two sides are authored on unrelated scales. A population centre contributes at most scale(<=5) x weight(<=0.60) x elasticity(<=2.50) = 7.5. The measured maximum demand fact across the whole world was 8.25 — demand is pinned at its structural ceiling, not at a level the economy chose. Verified independently against scripts/economy.lua's basket.
4. A vertically-integrated corp's real consumption never reaches demand at all: run_processing draws pool-first and records only the market-inventory remainder into report.purchases.

AND THE GATE IS INVERTED. `if (demand <= 0.0f) return 1.0f;` reads as humility — 'no signal, do not guess' — and is the bug: the slots with no demand signal ARE the real gluts, and they are exactly the ones that escape penalty. The gate fires only where a token signal happens to exist.

ONE REAL DIMENSIONAL DEFECT was found, in the consumer rather than the fields: projected_supply compares ONE tick of existing supply against HORIZON ticks of added supply (horizon = build_duration + 1, so roughly 3x). DECISION TAKEN, and it is a decision not to act: it was NOT fixed in isolation. It is a genuine defect and a small edit, but fixing it moves every blessed golden (it changes build scoring, hence world evolution), and paying that to correct the numerator of a gate whose denominator is not a constraint buys only a different set of wrong vetoes. It is folded into BL-381 to be fixed in one re-bless alongside the denominator.

The harness is complicit and is named in the item: corp_ai_predictive_harness asserts the taper band against hand-set fixtures (demand 1000 / supply 0; demand 100 / supply 10) that no generated world can reach. It has been green the whole time against a shape the game does not produce, which is why none of this surfaced.

A THIRD saturated consumer was found on verification, and it is the strongest argument in the item: dispatch_convoys gates inter-body hauls on `dest.demand - dest.supply > 0`, so the same mismatch suppresses INTER-BODY CONVOY DISPATCH — the logistics layer, not just an AI gate. Corroborated independently by data_creep_harness, whose coverage section reports auto-dispatch never firing across a 3000-tick rollout, previously attributed to the launchpad gate alone.

The candidate real denominator already exists and this entry did not know about it: market_component.inventory (BL-130) is persistent, drains against production and construction, and grows when nothing consumes it. A rising inventory is what a glut actually looks like in this economy. Whether to re-point the forecast at inventory, or instead make demand real by giving the offstage economy a consumption model that scales with production rather than with population scale, is the open decision — filed as BL-381 (priority A), because it is an ECONOMY call as much as an AI one. Two inert market writes found alongside are BL-382.

items.title: ai_skill_harness could not name six of the fifteen corp verbs, and its thrash ceilings were blessed against the thrashing behaviour they exist to catch
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI gameplay session.
items.what: The harness's verb_name switch stopped at hire_unit, so the BL-293 order-book verbs, set_workforce_auto and the three BL-350 procurement verbs all pooled into a single action[?] row — 7-8 actions per rollout that turned out to be place_sell_order, i.e. the AI's entire trading behaviour was unnamed in its own skill instrument. Fixed: the switch is now exhaustive over corp_verb, so -Wswitch guards it the next time the seam grows. Two further switches in corp_ai.cpp had the same omission and are also now exhaustive -- corp_verb_label was narrating a contract decision into the world history log as 'ordered a action', and the agency_event mapping had NO default at all, so an unhandled verb would have kept agency_event's zero-initialised kind and narrated a procurement as 'switched recipe' (a wrong statement rather than a missing one). Separately, the dial-thrash ceilings (230-410 per seed) pass comfortably against rollouts containing 134-255 resumes, because they were blessed FROM a run of the thrashing behaviour — the detector certifies the defect it was built to find.
items.why_it_matters: Both are the same failure in different clothes: a golden blessed from observed behaviour encodes whatever the behaviour was, including its bugs, and a tally that cannot name a verb cannot band it either. The project's convention that goldens are disposable and re-blessed routinely is right, but it means the blessing moment is the only point where anyone asks whether the observed number is the number that SHOULD be observed, and for these ceilings nobody did. Worth a rule rather than a one-off fix: a thrash ceiling in particular should be argued from the action budget (corps x evals x max_dials) rather than blessed from a run. Update 2026-08-13: the ceilings have now been tightened from 230-410 to 40-69 against corrected behaviour, so this specific instance is closed; the RULE (derive a thrash ceiling from the action budget rather than blessing it from a run) is what remains open.
options: Derive the dial ceiling from the budget arithmetic instead of blessing it from a run, so it binds on the first regression rather than the second.
Add the resume-to-idle ratio as its own banded metric (see NR-178 option 3).
Leave the ceilings as observation-blessed and rely on the printed tally being read by a human each time.
items.recommendation: Options 1 and 2 together, next time the corp-AI arc is opened. Neither is urgent, and both are cheap once someone is already re-blessing this file.

items.title: The action dictionary is four verbs behind the seam it is transcribed from — hire_unit and the three procurement verbs have no entry
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI gameplay session, found while repairing the --serve seam.
items.what: docs/ai/ACTIONS.json's gameplay family holds 11 entries against corp_command.hpp's 15 verbs. Missing: hire_unit (BL-324), request_quote, accept_quote and cancel_contract (BL-350). CLAUDE.md's own rule for this store is explicit — the gameplay entries are TRANSCRIBED from corp_command.hpp rather than authored, and 'where the dictionary and the seam disagree, the dictionary is wrong and the fix is mechanical'. Not fixed in this session because the entries are not in fact mechanical: each needs its real `press` (the UI path a player actually takes) and its `reason_to_select`, and writing those from the header alone would invent a UI that may not exist. The seam-side repair this session DID land, so all fifteen verbs are now reachable on the wire and only their documentation lags.
items.why_it_matters: AI_OPPONENT.md section 10a names the dictionary as the MEANING leg of the word interface, next to the blackboard (read) and the command seam (write). A verb absent from it is a verb an out-of-process policy is never told exists — so the practical effect of this gap is identical to the wire-level gap that was just fixed, one layer up. It is also the second time the same failure has appeared in one session: the seam grew, and three separate consumers (the --serve parser, ai_skill_harness's verb tally, this dictionary) each silently kept describing the older, smaller seam.
options: Write the four entries properly, which means first establishing whether hire_unit and the procurement verbs have a player-facing press at all — if they do not, that is itself the finding and the entries should say so.
Add a generated consistency check that fails when ACTIONS.json's gameplay family and corp_verb disagree — the mechanical half, without authoring prose.
Both: the check now, the prose when the verbs get their UI.
items.recommendation: Option 3, and note that option 2 is deliberately a CHECK rather than a generator. Ben's standing ruling on this store is that enforcement is authorship, not machinery ('the docs are the audit, we don't need an audit method', 2026-08-01) — that ruling was about not auto-verifying the question_log's prose, and a count mismatch against an enum is a different thing from grading wording. Worth confirming he reads it the same way before building it.
items.resolution:
RESOLVED 2026-08-13. Option 3's prose half taken, and the investigation it required produced the more interesting half of the answer.

The four entries are written and the dictionary is now at exact parity with the enum: 15 gameplay entries against 15 corp_verb values, zero drift in either direction (checked mechanically both ways). render_actions.js, which is also the store's shape check, regenerates clean.

THE FINDING, which this entry anticipated as a possibility and which turned out to be the case: the four verbs split two ways. `hire_unit` HAS a real player press — a 'Hire' list in the Selection info element on a tile carrying the player's own completed military base (selection_panel.cpp) — and got an ordinary entry. The three BL-350 procurement verbs have NO UI AT ALL: a grep of src/ui for request_quote / accept_quote / cancel_contract returns nothing. The seam, its world state, its serialisation and its harness all landed; the UI never did.

So their entries say so, plainly, and that is not a placeholder — an entry reading 'no human can press this, you can' is precisely what a language policy needs to know, and it makes the three verbs the first genuinely AGENT-ONLY controls in the game. Their `reason_to_select` fields are written for that reader: request_quote's four typed declines are documented as a cheap intelligence probe (it mutates nothing on a decline and each refusal names a different fact about a supplier), and cancel_contract's is written around the asymmetry that the forfeited deposit is a one-off you can price while the reputation move is persistent and resurfaces much later as rejected_reputation.

STILL OWED, deliberately: the mechanical consistency check (this entry's option 2). It is a few lines and would have caught this drift on the day it appeared. It is not built here because Ben's standing ruling on this store is that enforcement is authorship, not machinery ('the docs are the audit, we don't need an audit method', 2026-08-01) — that ruling was about not auto-grading the question_log's WORDING, and a count mismatch against an enum is a different kind of object, but the distinction is his to draw and not mine to assume. Left as the one open question on this entry.

items.title: The constraint-tax leg of the 2026-08-08 C-route ruling has been superseded in framing — the ruling still holds, but on its other legs
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI gameplay session; SOTA refresh over the window since the 2026-08-03 sweep.
items.what: AI_OPPONENT.md section 10g's ruling (Stage A/B stays the action generator; a language model must not emit corp_command as the shipped rival) rested on three arguments: (1) distilling corp_ai.cpp cannot exceed corp_ai.cpp, the behavioural-cloning ceiling; (2) legibility and determinism are named requirements; (3) the CONSTRAINT TAX -- small open-weight models measured dropping from 91.5% to 48.0% executable accuracy under a hard tool-call schema. Argument (3) has been reframed by later work. 'Capacity, Not Format' (arXiv 2606.09410) finds the penalty tracks a model's SPARE CAPACITY rather than the output format: Sonnet loses nothing under a hard schema, Haiku drops 36.2pp, GPT-4o-mini 28.0pp, and APIs that reason before serialising largely eliminate the tax. DECISION TAKEN on Ben's behalf: the ruling is left standing and NOT reopened, because arguments (1) and (2) are untouched and neither depends on a format penalty. What is recorded instead is the replacement: multi-turn tool-calling accuracy at Io's target model size is poor and is a STRONGER disqualifier than the constraint tax ever was -- xLAM-2-3B scores 55.62% multi-turn on BFCL v4 and Qwen3-4B 35.25%, against 62-66% single-turn, and one 4X turn is many sequential calls with compounding error.
items.why_it_matters: A ruling that quietly rests on a superseded finding is a ruling nobody can re-examine honestly later. The correction does not change the outcome, which is exactly why it is worth writing down now rather than when someone tries to reopen the question and finds the cited evidence has moved. Ben should know the argument he ruled on has a weaker third leg and a stronger replacement available.
options: Accept: amend section 10g's constraint-tax paragraph to cite the multi-turn tool-calling numbers instead, keeping the ruling.
Reopen the ruling on the grounds that one of its three legs weakened -- not recommended, since the other two are the load-bearing ones.
Leave both the ruling and its stated reasoning untouched and treat this entry as the record.
items.recommendation: Option 1, next time section 10 is edited. It is a citation swap, not a re-argument, and it leaves the ruling stronger than it was.

items.title: The --serve float parser admitted NaN and Inf into the order book, where a NaN price makes the market sort undefined behaviour
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI gameplay session; found by adversarial review of this session's own change, not by a failing test.
items.what:
Teaching --serve's COMMAND opcode to parse float arguments (needed to reach place_sell_order and the BL-350 procurement verbs at all) introduced a hole, because std::atof parses 'nan' and 'inf' happily and the seam's validation cannot catch either. place_sell_order's only price guard is `cmd.floor_price < 0.0f`, and every comparison against NaN is false, so a NaN price passed validation, entered world.sell_orders, was folded into world::state_hash, was written to the save stream, and reached clear_markets' book sort -- where a value that is neither less than, equal to nor greater than any other stops the comparator being a strict weak ordering, which makes std::sort undefined behaviour rather than merely wrong. An infinity survived every `> 0.0f` guard and then overflowed a static_cast<int> in request_quote's lead-time derivation. DECISIONS TAKEN: (1) non-finite values are refused at the parser and treated as if the key were absent, because the boundary is the only place that can distinguish 'the caller sent nonsense' from 'the value is legitimately zero'; (2) request_quote's lead time is clamped before narrowing, which protects every caller rather than just this one. 

CORRECTED 2026-08-13, same session, by the adversarial review's own verification pass: the first cut of the guard SUBSTITUTED the default instead of refusing, and that is a different bug rather than a fix. The two keys sharing kv_getf have defaults that mean opposite things downstream -- `quantity`'s 0 is rejected by the seam, so substituting it refuses by accident, but `floor_price`'s 0 is MEANINGFUL (the seam reads it as 'accept the market price'). So `floor_price=inf` turned 'sell only above this unreachable floor' -- effectively hold -- into 'sell up to quantity at market, every tick', answered `applied`, and issued no diagnostic. Reachable through the MCP server too, where a JSON 1e400 becomes Infinity and stringifies straight onto the wire past a `type: 'number'` schema. kv_getf now reports malformation through an `ok` out-param and the COMMAND handler answers rejected_invalid; tools/mcp/smoke.js asserts it for nan, inf and 1e400 on floor_price and for nan on quantity, so the two keys cannot drift apart again. 

THE GUARD WAS INCOMPLETE, found the same day by adversarial play, and it is worth recording because of how it failed rather than that it did. `kv_getf`'s check is `std::isfinite(v)` on the DOUBLE. `quantity=1e300` is a perfectly finite double, passes the guard, and then overflows to +INFINITY when narrowed to `float` on assignment to `cmd.quantity`. So the NaN hole was closed and the infinity hole beside it was left open, in the same function, in the same session, by the same author, while writing a comment about how important it was to validate at the boundary.

The precise lesson: 'validate at the boundary' means validate the value that ACTUALLY LANDS IN THE FIELD, not the intermediate you happened to parse. A range check against the destination type is the only form of it that holds. Folded into BL-396, which generalises it — the same parser truncates an out-of-range verb into a different verb and applies it, and segfaults on an out-of-range building type, so a checked-narrowing helper is needed for every field rather than a second special case for this one.
items.why_it_matters: It is worth recording as a decision rather than a fix because of where the hole came from. Nothing in the diff was careless -- the parser was added to close a real gap, and its guard was the same `< 0.0f` the rest of the seam uses. What made it dangerous is that the AI-facing seam is an UNTRUSTED input boundary in a way the UI is not: the UI's controls cannot emit a NaN, so the validation downstream of them never had to. Every future verb added to this protocol inherits that property, and the general rule -- validate at the protocol edge, not at the seam that assumed a UI wrote it -- is the thing to carry, not the two specific guards. The correction is the more instructive half: the fix was written, reviewed by its own author as obviously right, and was still wrong in a way that produced a WORSE failure mode than a crash -- a silently different order with a success code. It took an adversarial verifier reading the downstream meaning of a default value to see it. 'Treat malformed input as absent' is a reasonable-sounding convention that only holds when absent and malformed lead to the same place, and here they did not.
options: Accept as landed.
Go further and validate ranges (not just finiteness) at the protocol edge, so a caller cannot submit an absurd-but-finite quantity either.
Push the finiteness check down into apply_corp_command so every caller is covered, not just the --serve path.
items.recommendation: Accept, and consider option 3 when the seam next grows a float argument. The lead-time clamp already went into apply_corp_command for exactly that reason; the finiteness check stayed at the parser only because the UI genuinely cannot produce a NaN and adding a guard there would be dead code with a misleading comment.

items.title: Four claims written into code comments and docs this session were overstated, and the review that caught them is the practice worth keeping
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI gameplay session; adversarial review lens run over the session's own diff, specifically tasked with checking whether the change's claims were supportable.
items.what:
A review lens was pointed at the session's own assertions rather than at its code, and found four that did not survive contact with the source. All are now corrected in place. (1) 'Six of the fifteen verbs could not be issued at all' -- five were unreachable; hire_unit's unit_type defaults to 0, a VALID roster index, so it worked and could only ever raise row 0. The comment had explicitly denied the partly-supported reading that was in fact correct for that one verb. (2) 'Nothing else on this protocol yields a body id' -- the blackboard keys pool facts by (corp, body) and body_activity by body, so an agent could name bodies it already traded on; the true gap is narrower and more useful to state precisely (it cannot name a body it has no presence on, which is every body worth surveying). (3) 'Exhaustive now, so -Wswitch catches the next one the way it did not catch this one' -- -Wswitch was already enabled and HAD been warning on every compile; the build runs -Wall without -Werror and the warnings were simply ignored. The guard is the reader, not the flag. (4) 'resume at ~10x every other verb combined' -- it was ~2.7x combined and ~10x the next single verb. Separately, the protocol header comment rewritten to be 'in step with the enums' still gave wrong numeric ranges for building_type and resource_type, and now names the enums instead of hard-coding ranges that go stale. 

A FIFTH, found 2026-08-13 by the verification pass on the NR-129 refutation and fixed with it: corp_ai.cpp's muster-base block stated the ordinary build loop 'only ever proposes extraction_site/processing_facility'. It proposes extraction_site ONLY — processing_facility appears in that file solely in dial and scoring contexts, never as a build candidate. Pre-existing and harmless, but it is the same failure as the four above and it landed in the same file, which is the argument for the claims lens being a standing part of review rather than a one-off: three separate passes over this file each caught a different unsupported statement, and none of them was caught by a compiler, a test, or a reader who was not specifically looking.
items.why_it_matters: None of these changed what the code does, and every one of them would have entered the permanent record as fact. This project's documents ARE its audit (Ben, 2026-08-01), so an overstated claim in a comment is not a cosmetic problem -- it is a false entry in the only record anyone will read later, and three of these four were the kind of confident specific number that nobody re-derives. The practice that caught them was cheap and mechanical: a review lens given the diff and the single instruction to check whether each stated claim was supportable from the source, with no authoring context. It found things the correctness lens did not, because it was reading the prose rather than the logic. Worth repeating on any change that writes numbers into an authority doc.
options: Adopt a claims lens as a standing part of the review pass for changes that touch an authority doc or write measured figures into comments.
Rely on the existing verifier-review skill, extending its lens list to include claim-checking.
Treat this as a one-off and move on.
items.recommendation: Option 2 -- fold it into verifier-review as a named lens rather than standing up a separate practice, since that skill is already the pre-compile gate and already has a lens list. The instruction that worked was narrow: check every stated claim against the source, and report the ones that cannot be substantiated, including claims about what a compiler flag or a test would have caught.

items.title: Four harnesses in the ctest tier are failing, all pre-existing, and two of them had no entry
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI gameplay session; found running the ctest tier over an unrelated change.
items.what:
stack_capacity_harness asserts 'S.R3 non-extraction type stays capacity 1 on a rich tile' and gets 4. The assertion encodes the pre-BL-366 rule; BL-366 (aa42da2, multi-building tile stack cap + urban transform) made the non-extraction cap a function of tile COMPOSITION via non_extraction_stack_cap(tc.composition), so 4 is the intended answer on the composition the harness uses. The harness was not updated with the change. Confirmed pre-existing rather than caused by this session: placement_rules.cpp is not in this session's diff at all (git diff --name-only over the session's three commits lists main.cpp, corp_ai.cpp, corp_command.cpp, economy_system.*, building_profit.*, and tools/docs only). 

WIDENED 2026-08-13, after the full 68-test tier completed: there are FOUR known failures, not three. history_sim_harness fails six assertions (R7 the 0->1960 runtime budget, R3a/R3a2/R3a3 the campaign-and-stall trio, R3b supply decay alone not stopping conquest, R5 winter campaigns chosen rather than clocked). Confirmed pre-existing by the method SPRINTS.md prescribes rather than by inspection: a throwaway git worktree at 4e0118d (the pre-session commit) was configured and built from cold, and its history_sim_harness produced the IDENTICAL six failures. So the tier's standing state is 64/68 with data_creep_harness (NR-171), population_mvp (NR-170), stack_capacity_harness (this entry) and history_sim_harness all red, and until today two of the four had no record anywhere. 

TRIAGED AND THREE FIXED, 2026-08-13. The four were not one problem. THREE were harness-side, each encoding a rule the code had deliberately changed, and each is now fixed: stack_capacity S.R3 asserted a constant cap of 1 that BL-366 superseded with a per-composition ceiling (re-authored to test the invariant it was actually written for — that richness must not leak into a non-extraction cap — which is strictly stronger than the constant and cannot be silently invalidated again); population_mvp R4 measured an empty demand basket rather than an absent population (NR-170); and data_creep R1's plateau window was pinned inside the build-out (NR-145). Roughly forty lines in total, and each restored a check that was previously testing nothing.

THE FOURTH is not a stale harness and is now filed as BL-384 (priority A): history_sim reports 267 battles and ZERO conquests across 1960 years — the political map is produced entirely by settlement and war moves no border at all. No assertion covers conquest count, which is exactly why six red assertions never surfaced it, and one of those six (R3b2) passes VACUOUSLY because its fixture never scores any campaign. NR-177 makes this sim the ancient product's generator, so it is not an Era -1 curiosity. 

CONFIRMED 2026-08-13 after the three fixes: the tier runs **59/60** (excluding the four long generation sweeps), with history_sim_harness the only red. Down from four failures to one, and the survivor is now EXPLAINED — BL-384 owns the defect underneath it — rather than being an unattributed red that trains people to read past the gate.
items.why_it_matters: Four unexplained reds, two of them unrecorded, is the state SPRINTS.md described as 'the gate went from lying to green' running in reverse. v0.1.10 closed with 55 tests and 0 failures -- the first fully green gate of the arc -- and the tier has since drifted back to a place where a full run means nothing without someone who remembers which reds are expected. That knowledge currently lives in one person's head and in two review entries filed today. The specific failures matter less than the fact that the tier no longer answers the question it exists to answer: did I break something? This session could only answer it by excluding the slow tests, running a scoped subset, and then building a pre-session worktree to adjudicate the one remaining doubt -- which is three steps too many for a routine change.
options: Re-tier the way v0.1.8 did: fix what should pass, and mark the rest expected-failing WITH the entry that explains why, so a red tier means something again.

Fix the four individually -- stack_capacity S.R3 is a one-line update to the BL-366 rule, and history_sim's six look like genuine drift in the Era -1 sim worth understanding before the 0 CE refocus leans on it.
Add a CTest label for known-failing and exclude it from the routine gate, keeping a separate command that runs everything.
Leave as is and rely on the review entries.
items.recommendation:
Two of the three parts are done. The three stale harnesses are fixed and the tier is 59/60. BL-384 owns the real defect under the remaining red.

The known-failing LABEL (option 3) is deliberately NOT taken here, and the reason is worth stating rather than leaving as an omission. It is a change to how the project's gate reports, which is Ben's call and not a side effect of a triage pass. More pointedly: this session found that the AI's thrash detector had been certifying the very oscillation it existed to catch, because its ceilings were blessed from a run of the broken behaviour. Adding machinery that marks a red as expected, in the same session, would be the same mistake one level up. The argument FOR the label is real — a gate with an unexplained red cannot answer 'did I break something?' — but that argument is much weaker now that the red is attributed to a filed priority-A item. Recommend deciding it deliberately, and if taken, requiring that every entry on the known-failing list names the backlog item that owns it.

items.title: A requirement can certify a defect, and then every downstream check confirms it — three instances of that shape in one day
items.source: 2026-08-13 AI-play session; found triaging BL-386.
items.what:
BL-386 (a sell order's floor price is paid in full by nobody, unbounded) is not code drifting from a specification. It IS the specification. requirements.json group `player-sell-orders` row R2, status COMPLETE, reads: 'A standing player sell order sells up to its quantity from the (corp, body) pool, valued at max(resolved_price, floor_price).' MARKETS.md step 11 states the same and calls it a prototype invariant. So the requirement was written, the code was built to match, the requirement was verified against the code, and the authority doc blessed the result — and the thing they all agreed on prints money.

The action dictionary managed to hold BOTH readings at once: its place_sell_order entry asserted `max(price, floor)` in one clause and 'a floor above what the resolution supports means less or nothing sells' in the next. Nobody noticed the contradiction because each half reads correct on its own.

THREE INSTANCES OF THE SAME SHAPE IN ONE SESSION, which is why this is filed as a pattern rather than as a note on BL-386: (1) this — a requirement that certifies the defect; (2) NR-181 — ai_skill_harness's thrash ceilings blessed FROM a run of the oscillation they exist to detect, so the detector certified it; (3) NR-185 — four confident measured claims in code comments and docs that nobody re-derived, plus a fifth found later. In every case the artifact that was supposed to catch the problem had been calibrated on the problem.
items.why_it_matters:
The project's verification culture is unusually strong — requirements, goldens, harnesses, a review skill, a documented claim discipline — and all of it shares one blind spot: an artifact authored FROM observed behaviour inherits whatever that behaviour was, including its bugs, and thereafter defends it. A golden blessed from a broken run, a requirement written from what the code does, and a comment stating a number nobody re-derived are the same failure wearing three costumes. The common trigger is that the authoring moment is the ONLY point at which anyone asks whether the observed thing is the thing that should be observed, and at that moment the author is usually the same person who just wrote the behaviour.

Worth noting what DID catch all three: an agent with no authoring context, either playing the game or reading the claims cold. That is a cheap and repeatable check, and it found in one session what the existing culture had been confirming for months.
options: Adopt the rule that a requirement is written BEFORE the behaviour it describes, never from it — the Delivery lifecycle already says step 0 comes first, so this is enforcement rather than new method.

Add a standing 'cold reader' pass to Full-mode delivery: one agent, no authoring context, asked only whether each stated claim and each blessed number is the one that SHOULD hold. Cheap, and it is what found all three.
Treat it as three separate fixes (rewrite R2, derive the ceilings, correct the claims) and not as a pattern.
Accept the blind spot as the cost of a fast prototype and rely on play sessions to surface it periodically.
items.recommendation: Options 1 and 2 together, and 2 is the cheaper of the two to start. The cold-reader pass costs one agent and found a priority-S economy defect, a certifying golden and five overstated claims in a single session — better yield than any other check run today. Option 1 is right in principle but harder to enforce, because the pressure to write the requirement after the fact is strongest exactly when the work is nearly done. Option 3 misses that these keep recurring; option 4 is defensible only if play sessions become routine, which NR-167 and AI_OPPONENT.md section 10h now argue they should.

items.title: BL-367 (multi-building management surface) landed without a live side-by-side screenshot of the grouped-stack list and the +N badge
items.source: BL-367 delivery session.
items.what: Implemented the grouped-by-stack list (construction_panel.cpp draw_tile_stack_list), the Manage-button/canvas-marker tile-routing fix, and the on-canvas +N badge (body_surface_canvas.cpp), per the item's 2026-08-11 settled design. Verified: ProjectIo builds clean, launches without crash (Lua loads, no render error in the startup log). NOT verified: an actual screenshot of a real multi-building tile showing the grouped list and the badge rendered correctly (correct stagger vs the corp-identity tag, correct text fit) — building a multi-building save state and driving the UI to it was out of scope for this pass.
items.why_it_matters: A UI feature that compiles and launches can still misrender (text overlap, badge collision, wrong stack ordering) in a way only a live screenshot catches — the standing practice (CLAUDE.md, DEVELOPMENT_PRACTICES.md) is to open the live app for exactly this kind of visual call.
options: Build a quick fixture (place several buildings on one tile via the construction ledger in a live session or a headless harness) and capture a screenshot of the grouped list + badge.
Wait for BL-365s background firms (which routinely produce multi-building tiles) to surface a real one in the next live session and check it there.
items.recommendation: Option 2 is cheap and likely soon — BL-365s ~80 background firms make multi-building tiles common in any fresh campaign now, so the next live session should hit one without deliberately constructing a fixture.

items.title: The stepped decision clock is NOT behaviour-neutral — a 100-year band never reaches Invest at all
items.source: Measured while landing the 4000 BCE stepped clock (Ben's 2026-08-12 steer), tools/verify/stepped_clock_harness.cpp R6
items.what: The stepped clock was designed on the assumption that scaling each per-year RATE by its band width makes a run roughly invariant to band choice — a 100-year band credits 100x per round and therefore lands in about the same place as a 1-year band. MEASUREMENT REFUTES THAT. Holding the world, the seed and the 4000-year span fixed and varying ONLY the band width: a 100-year band (40 decision rounds) accrues tech credit of exactly ZERO, while a 20-year band (200 rounds) accrues 146,440. Invest is not under-credited at 100 years; it is never CHOSEN at 100 years. Sampling the world at 40 moments rather than 200 changes which verb wins the argmax at each moment, and with Settle dominating the comparison the coarse run settles at every single one (459 foundings, 0 battles, 0 conquests across the default ladder run).
items.why_it_matters: Two things follow, and the second is the expensive one. (1) The band ladder cannot be treated as a transparent performance optimisation — it is a design parameter that changes what history the generator produces, so the boundaries have to be tuned against outcomes rather than picked for tidiness. The current default ladder (100/50/20/10/5/1) spends its two coarsest bands, 3000 of the 4000 years, in the regime where Invest is never selected. (2) The underlying cause is NOT the stepped clock. It is BL-318 (shared-currency scorer): history_sim.hpp already records that the four verbs are scored on incommensurable scales, that BL-309's normalisation attempt was reverted, and that the observed failure mode was exactly a Settle-dominated run with conquests at zero. The stepped clock did not introduce this; it made it visible and it amplifies it at coarse bands.
options: Tune the band boundaries so the coarse bands are narrower (e.g. start the 20-year band earlier), accepting more decision rounds for better-behaved history.
Land BL-318 (shared-currency scorer) first, then re-measure the ladder against a scorer where Invest can actually win.
Accept a settle-dominated deep prehistory as correct — 4000-2000 BCE arguably SHOULD be mostly settlement expansion rather than investment or war.
items.recommendation: Option 3 is more defensible than it first looks and should be considered before spending anything: a world whose earliest two millennia are dominated by settling new ground, with little war and little technological investment, is a plausible neolithic-to-bronze-age shape rather than a bug. But it should be a CHOSEN outcome, not one inherited from a scorer defect that history_sim.hpp already documents as unresolved. So: decide whether the deep-prehistory shape is what is wanted, and if it is, record that here so BL-318's eventual fix does not silently overturn it.
items.resolution: ANSWERED (Ben, 2026-08-12): option 3 — a settle-dominated deep prehistory is CORRECT and intended, not a defect to tune around. The band ladder stays as proposed (100/50/20/10/5/1 over 4000 BCE -> 0 CE), and the two coarsest bands spending 3000 of the 4000 years in a settle-only regime is the shape wanted: the neolithic-to-bronze-age stretch should be expansion into new ground rather than war or investment. RECORDED SO IT IS NOT SILENTLY OVERTURNED: when BL-318 (shared-currency scorer) lands and Invest can win the argmax on its own merits, the deep-prehistory bands must be re-checked against THIS ruling rather than allowed to drift into a war-and-invest early history by side effect. The stepped clock is therefore accepted as non-behaviour-neutral by design.

items.title: Two gate harnesses were already failing before the 3x map change, for unrelated reasons
items.source: Found while verifying the 3x map / stepped-clock work (Ben, 2026-08-12); ctest -LE sweep, 63 of 67 passed
items.what: The gate reported four failures. TWO ARE PRE-EXISTING and grid-independent, established by inspection rather than assumed. (1) stack_capacity_harness S.R3 'non-extraction type stays capacity 1 on a rich tile' gets 4, wants 1, five times. The harness builds a SYNTHETIC tile_component and calls placement_rules::stack_capacity directly — it never touches the tile grid — and placement_rules.cpp is unmodified, so no map change can reach it. Something widened stack capacity to non-extraction building types without updating this assertion. (2) population_mvp R4 'Kepler market.demand[agricultural_produce] > 0' gets 0 across ALL 11 Kepler markets. Cause: the harness constructs an EMPTY recipe_registry on the comment 'empty -- population injection runs unconditionally', which was true until BL-368 generalised inject_population_demand into a per-centre basket read from reg.population_demand(). population_demand_params::demand_basket is zero-initialised, so an empty registry injects nothing on any grid of any size.
items.why_it_matters: Both were misattributable to the map change and neither is caused by it — an incorrect attribution would have sent someone hunting a generation bug that does not exist. More importantly, each is a harness whose assertion has quietly stopped describing the product: stack_capacity_harness encodes a rule the code no longer follows, and population_mvp encodes a setup contract BL-368 retired. A red gate that is mostly stale assertions is the exact failure mode v0.1.8 was cut to fix (NR-103's finding, and BL-288's 'the suite reported ten failures; exactly one was a failing assertion'). These two are how it comes back.
options: Fix both harnesses: give population_mvp a real demand basket, and update stack_capacity_harness S.R3 to the rule the code actually implements (or fix the code if the widening was unintended).

Fix population_mvp only — its setup contract is unambiguously stale — and triage stack_capacity_harness separately, since 'capacity 4 on a non-extraction type' may be a real defect rather than a stale test.
File both as backlog items and leave the gate red until they are scheduled.
items.recommendation: Option 2. population_mvp is a clear-cut stale setup contract and cheap to fix. stack_capacity_harness is NOT obviously stale — BL-193's design deliberately left 'whether processors stack' as a deferred question, and the assertion says richness must not leak into that answer. Getting 4 instead of 1 may well be richness leaking exactly as the comment warned, in which case the code is wrong and the test is right. Do not touch that assertion until someone has read stack_capacity's current implementation against BL-193's intent.

items.title: BL-253 was already fixed; the 3x-map tick cost is run_economy_step, and econ_stability cannot see it
items.source: Measured while acting on Ben's 2026-08-12 instruction to fix BL-253
items.what: Asked to fix BL-253 (the O(corps x tiles) strategic scan), I found it ALREADY COMPLETE — rank_extraction_sites was hoisted out of the per-corp loop and the code says so. The real cost was elsewhere. Two safe micro-optimisations to that function (memoising the per-tile body lookup, partial_sort instead of a full sort of ~18,000 sites to keep ~64) are correct and behaviour-identical but moved the needle NOT AT ALL: 300/600-tick rollouts stayed at 47s/105s. A new tools/verify/tick_profile.cpp then answered it in one run: run_economy_step is 89.7% of the tick, with clear_markets a distant 8.1% and everything else — convoys, orbits, budget, surveys — under 1.2% combined. | DECISION TAKEN 2026-08-12, reversible: data_creep_harness is PARKED out of the routine gate (CMakeLists sweep label). Sequence, so the reasoning is not lost — the 240s LONG tier was outgrown; a new 1200s XLONG tier was added and the run exceeded THAT too, because per-tick cost rises as buildings accumulate and the 4500-tick tail is far dearer than a 300/600-tick sample projects. Trimming ticks to fit was rejected (a plateau measured before saturation keeps the test green while emptying it) and raising the bound a second time is the exact treadmill that section exists to refuse. The sweep section header was amended to distinguish TWO reasons a harness lands there: a research sweep whose cost is the point, versus a parked regression check that is a DEBT.
items.why_it_matters: Three things. (1) The instrument that exists to catch this is blind to it: econ_stability sweeps bodies x corps and NEVER varies tile count, so it reported 0.09 ms/tick and a healthy sub-linear 0.85 exponent while the real rollout went from ~4.7 to ~165 ms/tick. Both numbers were true and they measured different things. (2) Two rounds of plausible guessing (the BL-253 site, then micro-optimising it) produced no improvement; one profiling run localised it. The profiler is now committed so the next such question costs one run. (3) The absolute figures are DEBUG-tree numbers — BL-288 records that build/ is deliberately Debug and econ_stability already SKIPs its absolute assertion for that reason — so the 50x is inflated and the Release figure is unknown. | THE GATE NOW HAS NO DATA-CREEP COVERAGE. That is a real hole and it is why this entry is a decision-taken rather than an observation: the fix is to restore the tick cost, never to edit the exclusion list.
options: Extend econ_stability's sweep to vary TILE COUNT as a third axis, so the blind spot closes permanently.
Profile run_economy_step internally (it is 90% of the tick) with a real recipe registry — tick_profile currently uses an empty one, so its absolute numbers understate production work.
Measure in Release before optimising anything further — the Debug amplification may be most of the apparent regression.
items.recommendation: Option 3 first, then 1. Optimising against Debug numbers risks tuning for an artefact, and it is the cheapest of the three to answer. Then extend econ_stability along the tile axis, because the blind spot is the reason a 50x real-world regression could sit behind a green performance gate at all — that is worth more than any single optimisation.

items.title: Generation is a stepping stone — AI players should start worlds, and the scorer should not be gold-plated until then
items.source: Ben, 2026-08-12, mid-session while tuning the Era -1 sim into generation
items.what: Ben, on being shown that the wired-in year-tick sim produced only modest turmoil: "Perhaps we can try instructing supply hubs? I think simplistic generation is just a stepping stone, we will want to use AI players to start worlds in the future." The supply-hub half was acted on immediately and is described in the resolution. The strategic half is the important part and is recorded here so it is not lost: procedural pre-history is EXPLICITLY temporary scaffolding, and the intended end state is AI players actually PLAYING the run-up to the campaign rather than a scored-utility loop approximating it.
items.why_it_matters: It sets the investment ceiling on a body of work that would otherwise absorb unbounded effort. The Era -1 scorer has now had three separate defects traced through it in one session (flat w_cult vetoing all war, flat w_dist not scaling with the map, capital-bound supply reach), and BL-318 names a fourth that is unresolved by design. Each is individually fixable and the pile has no natural end — because a utility scorer approximating a player is being asked to produce something only a player produces. Knowing the destination is AI players changes the correct response from "keep tuning" to "make it good enough to play against, then replace it". It also means the sim's ARCHITECTURE matters more than its constants, which is what BL-271's transfer contract already says.
items.recommendation: Treat the current state as the stepping stone it is: 62 battles / 16 conquests over 400 years is alive rather than inert, and that is the bar it had to clear. Do NOT pursue BL-318 for its own sake. When the AI-player route is designed, it should read AI_OPPONENT.md § 10 (the small local model over the word interface) alongside BL-271's transfer contract — an AI player starting worlds is the same seam as an AI player contesting one, and building it twice would be the waste.
items.resolution: ACTED ON, 2026-08-12. (1) SUPPLY HUBS, done: campaign supply was measured from the polity's CAPITAL, so reach was a property of empire shape rather than frontier presence and a large polity could not attack its own border. It now projects from the staging holding adjacent to the target - which the loop was already standing in - so reach is bounded by neighbour_radius and cannot blow up when the map does. Real world: 39 -> 62 battles. This also let an earlier map-width-derived supply_decay workaround be REMOVED rather than kept. (2) STEPPING-STONE FRAMING, recorded: no further scorer work is scheduled. Settling still dominates (1107 foundings against 16 conquests) and that is left standing deliberately, per this ruling, rather than tuned away. The AI-players-start-worlds direction is filed here as the successor rather than as an item, because it needs designing against AI_OPPONENT.md § 10 before it can be scoped.

items.title: The startup crash resists four progressively faithful reproductions; permanent crash reporting added so the next manual repro names the fault
items.source: This session, working NEXT_SESSION.md Task 1 (the startup crash)
items.what: The handoff said: get the actual error before hypothesising. A double-clicked exe has no console, so DECISION 1: the app now writes every death shape to build/crash.log — the fatal-error catch in main() mirrors its message there (it previously went only to invisible stderr), a SetUnhandledExceptionFilter names hardware faults (access violation / stack overflow, code + address), and a std::set_terminate handler catches exceptions escaping noexcept boundaries or threads. DECISION 2: a new --autostart-windowed mode drives the REAL interactive path under a terminal — real SDL window, real ImGui frames, walks the wizard round by round (with rerolls, so resolved params leave the default family), presses Begin from inside the wizard frame (the exact button call site), rides the loading screen through the mid-frame start_new_game transition, then injects synthetic centre-screen clicks on the first five in-game frames (the impatient-player clicks Windows queues during the stall) and renders 120 in-game frames. RESULT: four runs — plain windowed Begin, walked wizard, walked wizard + first-frame clicks, walked wizard + rerolls + clicks — ALL complete clean, exit 0, no crash.log. Combined with the previous session (headless generation per seed, async worker, statics sweep, --autostart tail, concurrent generations all clean), the crash now has no reproduction on any automated path.
items.why_it_matters: The strongest lead in the handoff — start_new_game resetting app state mid-ImGui-frame — is now MEASURED CLEAN, not just reasoned about: the wizard-walking run makes exactly that transition with real frames and survives. What remains is only what automation cannot supply: Ben-specific wizard inputs (his particular leans/seed), sustained human mouse activity, or an EXTERNAL kill — and the last is a live hypothesis worth holding: Smart App Control / Defender terminating a fresh unsigned exe mid-run leaves no C++ trace at all, and this machine already blocks fresh harness exes (the WSL memory). crash.log disambiguates every case on the next manual repro: a fatal-error line means a data/logic throw, a hardware-exception line means a real fault with an address, a terminate line means a thread/noexcept escape, and an EMPTY crash.log beside a dead process now positively indicates external termination (or a Debug assert dialog) rather than a program bug.
options: Ben reproduces once from a terminal (or double-click, then reads build/crash.log) and hands back the one line — the intended next step.
Sweep wizard-preference combinations through --autostart-windowed (each run ~40 s) if the log implicates generation params.
If crash.log is empty at the next repro, check Windows Event Viewer (Application log) for the exit code and Defender/SAC history before touching the code.
items.recommendation: Option 1. The reproduction battery is saved and cheap to rerun; guessing further without the log would repeat the exact mistake the handoff warns against. Note the loading screen now also draws the Task-2 inner year bar, so the next manual run doubles as its visual check.
items.resolution: ROOT CAUSE FOUND, 2026-08-12, same session, after Ben reproduced a second time (died at Finishing). Windows Error Reporting held the answer the crash handlers could not: every death today (17:07, 17:15, 17:38, 20:16) is an AppHangB1 — 'stopped interacting with Windows and was closed'. It was never a crash: the post-generation tail froze the UI, the player clicked, Windows killed the process. The tail was measured (new per-phase accumulators, step_economy_phase_ms): the 80-tick warm start took ~90 s, of which persona counsel was 83.9 s (93%) — export_corp_blackboard + the Lua bench per due corp per tick, at 35 corps since BL-365. Fixes landed: (1) counsel suppressed during the warm start (m_warm_starting — its output was advisory chat for pre-game quarters, all stamped on one day); (2) the warm start now runs in 50 ms slices, one batch per loading-screen frame, with the inner bar showing year N/20 — the UI repaints throughout, so Windows can never judge the app hung, whatever a tick costs; (3) two logistics scaling fixes found on the way (reach-field anchor-set precompute; invalidation narrowed to port/hub/road events). Warm start: ~90 s -> ~6.5 s, and un-hangable. The in-game counsel cost remains open as BL-398 (persona counsel tick cost); the crash logger stays — it correctly proved by silence that no fault ever fired.

items.title: The startup 'crash' was Windows killing a hung app; the warm start is now sliced and the loading screen honest — two behaviour notes for review
items.source: This session, after the AppHangB1 diagnosis (NR-209 resolution)
items.what: Two decisions taken in the fix, both reversible. (1) PERSONA COUNSEL IS SKIPPED during the 80-tick pre-game warm start (app.cpp, m_warm_starting): it was 83.9 s of the 90 s stall, and what it produced there was 80 quarters of advisory chat all stamped on the same pre-game day — counsel for events the player never saw. Live play still posts counsel every eval boundary. The Counsel channels therefore open EMPTY now rather than pre-filled with warm-up chatter; nation agency comms (cheap, 10 ms) still post through the warm start, unchanged. (2) INVALIDATION NARROWED (logistics.hpp): Ben's 2026-08-08 'clear on every event' rule assumed events are rare; the corp AI now builds/idles per tick, so the sim-rate call sites gate on building_affects_logistics (port/inland hub only — nothing else can change an anchor or a traversal cost). Road placement still clears unconditionally; player-rate UI sites keep the unconditional clear. Also: the reach-field seed no longer calls is_supply_anchor per grid cell (was O(tiles x (centres+buildings)) — ~50M probes per rebuild at 0 CE scale), it precomputes the identical anchor set once.
items.why_it_matters: Both change observable behaviour at the margins. (1) is visible in the chat panel: no pre-game counsel history. If Ben WANTS the bench to narrate the warm-up (it does establish voice), the flag is one condition — but then BL-398 must land first or the stall returns. (2) is the reversal of a recorded ruling, taken on Ben's own 'go for it from a code review angle' steer; the reasoning is in logistics.hpp's comment so the next reader sees why the simple rule bent. The narrowing is provably answer-preserving (no other building type can appear in the anchor set, and traversal cost reads only road_level/landform/composition), so the risk is a future building type that anchors supply and forgets to join building_affects_logistics.
options: Accept both as landed (recommended).
Restore warm-start counsel behind BL-398 once its cost is bounded.
Revert the invalidation narrowing if a future anchor-type building makes the type-gate fragile; the perf then rests on BL-398-class work instead.
items.recommendation: Accept. The loading screen is now honest end-to-end: generation bar -> ancient-era year bar -> 'Letting the dust settle' year 0-20 -> play, with no window where the app stops pumping. Verify visually on the next launch (the visual eyeball this session could not do).
